turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Morning. Have a seat. I'll get your vitals and peek at the medicine list before the doctor comes in.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. I hope coming a little early is no trouble. The parking lot was rather full today.
[SEG0003] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): You're fine. Blood pressure is one fifty-two over eighty-eight. Pulse seventy-six. Oxygen ninety-seven percent.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): That reading seems a little high. My daughter usually writes these figures down for me.
[SEG0005] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): She didn't come with you?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): No. She lives with me and she manages the pill box, but she has a shift at the library this morning.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): The branch on Maple, if that is of interest. She has worked there a good while.
[SEG0008] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): On the list I have furosemide forty milligrams daily, lisinopril, aspirin, and a potassium pill. What are you actually taking?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): If I may put it in my own words. There is the water tablet, the little white one, and my aspirin. The potassium I never—
[SEG0010] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Sorry, the scale. You weigh one hundred eighty-four pounds. Go ahead.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. The potassium I never started. The pharmacy held it, and I did not collect it.
[SEG0012] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): All right, no potassium. The water tablet, what dose?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Twenty milligrams— well, actually, twenty milligrams in the morning. My daughter also puts a Lasix in the box, another little tablet, so I may be taking two.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Morning. Dr. Ellison. You're here for the swelling?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, Doctor. My ankles have been swelling. I ought to have come sooner, but the weeks got away from me.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): When did it start?
[SEG0017] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I'll leave the list on the chart. Furosemide is down as forty milligrams.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): As I was saying, last winter, or it may have been the winter before. I cannot give you a proper date, and I apologize.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Both legs?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Both ankles, and it creeps up toward the shins by evening.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Short of breath?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): When I walk out to the mailbox, yes. Not while I am at rest. I do have to pause on the path.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Chest pain?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None at all.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Cough? Any fever?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough. I have not felt feverish.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Water pill every day?

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): I believe so. Though, well, some evenings a tablet is still sitting in the slot. My daughter fills the box on Sundays. I am not entirely sure I take every dose as I should.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Chart says forty milligrams of furosemide. You said twenty.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Twenty of the water tablet, and Lasix besides, which I had thought was a different medicine. If they are the same, I have counted it twice. I feel rather foolish.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Same drug. What else is in the box?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Aspirin, eighty-one milligrams, one each morning. I have taken that for years.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): The little white one?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): For my blood pressure, one each morning. I have had high blood pressure for years. I do not know its name. It is simply the little white one, and my daughter would know.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): There was also the cholesterol tablet, atorvastatin, forty milligrams. Another doctor told me to stop it.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): When was that?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Last winter, or the one before. I cannot be certain which. I have not taken a single one since.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): And lisinopril, are you on it?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): It was prescribed, I believe, but I never took it. Not even once. It may still be sitting on your paper.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Swelling there in the morning, or only later?

[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Mostly by the afternoon. They are nearly flat when I rise. I sleep on two pillows, if that is useful, though my neighbor's husband does the same and that is neither here nor there.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me look. Hold still.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Of course, Doctor.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Pitting edema, both ankles, up over the shins. Lungs are clear. No redness.
[SEG0045] person_3 (DOCTOR): This is fluid retention. I'm setting the water pill at forty milligrams once each morning, by mouth. One tablet, not two.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand. One only.
[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll check a metabolic panel, kidneys and potassium. The lab can draw you today.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, Doctor. I am able to go downstairs.
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): Cut back the salt. Elevate your legs in the afternoon. Weigh yourself a few mornings a week.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): I will do that. Ought I to ask my daughter to redo the pill box?
[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes. Bring every bottle next time so we can name that white tablet. Don't start anything new.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Certainly. And the cholesterol tablet stays stopped?
[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): Leave it stopped. See me in two weeks.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Thank you. The bus runs quite regularly, so that will be manageable.
[SEG0055] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I can walk you to the lab for the blood draw whenever you're ready.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): That is very kind. I do hope I have not taken too much of the morning.
[SEG0057] person_3 (DOCTOR): You're set.

spec.situation: Older patient with a live-in carer or daughter who manages the pill box; names of tablets are described ('the little white one', 'the water tablet'), one was stopped by another doctor, one is double-counted. Doctor reviews and changes one medicine.
features: stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.
doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).
vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.
interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

bad.reason: Transcript says lungs are clear, not that crackles were specifically assessed absent.
Doctor says no redness, but leg body site is not specified.
Medication discrepancy is discussed and resolved: doctor explains Lasix and furosemide are the same drug.
